UI.text: 12:39 45 TREND VIEW 1 Why Does Exercise Intensity Matter? Balancing time in different HR zones is key to developing your long-term fitness by making your cells stronger to facilitate more sustainable progress towards your fittest and healthiest years. Training in HR zones 1-3 helps you build your aerobic base—your body's ability to use oxygen efficiently during sustained activities like running and cycling, improving your endurance and long-term health. Prioritizing training in HR zones 1-3, rather than always pushing hard, maximizes your aerobic base-building efforts and supports your body's recovery and long- term performance. Exercising in HR zones 4-5 strengthens your heart, making it more efficient at pumping blood and adapting to intense demands. At the same time, this trains your body to perform short, high-intensity bursts, like sprinting. It improves your anaerobic capacity—the ability to sustain and recover from demanding efforts. It also increases your V02 Max, a key measure of your fitness and long-term health. w

UI.text: 12:39 45 TREND VIEW What is Heart Rate Zone Training? Heart rate (HR) zone training is an exercise method that focuses on tracking your heart rate during workouts and maintaining specific HR ranges. Training within these zones helps you manage workout intensity, boosting your cardiovascular health and overall fitness. On WHOOP, your HR zones are personalized to your unique physiology, based on your heart rate reserve (HRR): Heart Rate Reserve (HRR) = Max HR - RHR Since your HRR evolves as your fitness level changes, WHOOP adjusts your zones dynamically. • Zone 5 (90-100%): All out intensity • Zone 4 (80-89%): High • Zone 3 (70-79%): Moderate • Zone 2 (60-69%): Light • Zone I (40-59%): Very light 5 3 2 1 —x w Why Does Exercise Intensity Matter?

Understanding the Science of Tracking Calories Calories measure the number of calories that you burn per day. This is calculated based on an estimate of your Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR) and your heart rate throughout the day. Your BMR is estimated from the height, weight and gender in your profile. Generally, the more active you are, the more calories you will burn. If you consume more calories than you burn you will gain weight (muscle or fat), if you consume less than you burn you will lose weight, and if you match the two you will maintain your current weight. w

UI.text: 12:40 x 44 STRAIN VS. RECOVERY The WHOOP Strain score measures cardiovascular and muscular exertion, quantifying physical and mental stress on your body. Strain is tracked on a 0-21 scale for your entire day and specific activities. Inspired by Borg's Rating of Perceived Exertion, strain levels are: Light (0-9) Minimal exertion is being put on the body, which encourages active recovery. Moderate (10-13) Moderate exertion is being put on the body, which balances fitness gains and recovery. High (14-17) Increased exertion which builds fitness gains, but makes it more difficult for your body to recover the next day. All Out (18-21) Significant exertion which increases fitness gains, but puts your body at greater risk for injury or overtraining. Balancing Strain and Recovery 21.0 18.0 14.5 14.0 11.2 10.0 8.7 6.0

UI.text: 12:40 44 x STRAIN VS. RECOVERY Following the Optimal Strain recommendation means that your body will get the maximum fitness gains without carried fatigue the next day. However, staying within the Optimal Strain Zone is not always the right way to train. While it allows your body to acutely recover from the day's training stimulus, your training zone should align with your short- and long-term goals. For example, tapering--the act of acutely reducing training load to reduce fatigue prior to competition--increases performance, and typically places the athlete in the Restorative Zone. Spending too much time in that zone, however, will eventually lead to detraining and fitness loss. On the other end of the spectrum, training in the Overreaching Zone day after day can lead to burnout, non-functional overreaching/overtraining syndrome, or injury. But, sequencing brief periods of overreaching and restorative training can create a supercompensation effect, and therefore can be a highly efficient way to train. In summary, no training zone is inherently "good" or "bad." The suitability of each zone depends on your specific goals.
